entries.title: wp_img_tag_add_decoding_attr() deprecated in WP 6.4: use wp_img_tag_add_loading_optimization_attrs()
entries.summary: The wp_img_tag_add_decoding_attr() function was deprecated in WordPress 6.4.0 in favor of wp_img_tag_add_loading_optimization_attrs(), which consolidates image optimization (decoding, loading, fetchpriority). Themes and plugins still using the old function will trigger deprecation notices on WP 6.4+. Replace calls with the new function.
entries.test_step:
1. On a WP 6.4.0+ site, search theme/plugin code for `wp_img_tag_add_decoding_attr(` calls.
2. Enable debug.log (WP_DEBUG = true) and check for deprecation notices.
3. Replace with `wp_img_tag_add_loading_optimization_attrs()` or remove the call and let WordPress handle optimization automatically.
4. Confirm no deprecation notices; verify images still render correctly.

entries.title: Escaping data at output prevents XSS: use context-correct escape functions
entries.summary: WordPress requires escaping (sanitizing) data at the output boundary to prevent XSS attacks. Use esc_html() for HTML content, esc_attr() for HTML attributes, esc_url() for URLs, and esc_js() for JavaScript. Always escape late, as you output, not early in the request lifecycle.
entries.test_step:
1. Search theme/plugin code for echo/print statements with variable interpolation.
2. For each output line, identify the context: HTML content, attribute, URL, or JavaScript.
3. Apply the appropriate escape function:
   - esc_html() for <tag>content</tag>
   - esc_attr() for attribute="value"
   - esc_url() for href/src/action
   - esc_js() for JavaScript / data-json contexts
   - wp_kses_post() for user-generated content that may contain safe HTML
4. Test in browser; verify no output corruption; run OWASP-ZAP or similar XSS test.

entries.title: A committed .env exposes secrets: rotating them is the fix, untracking the file is not
entries.summary: Environment files (.env) holding API keys, database passwords or licence keys must never be committed to git. Once one has been pushed, treat every credential in it as public and rotate it: that is the only step that actually ends the exposure. git rm --cached stops tracking the file going forward and leaves every past commit intact, so the secret stays readable in history, in clones and in forks. Purging it needs a history rewrite with git-filter-repo plus a force push, and GitHub warns that clones and forks may keep copies even then. Add .env to .gitignore, keep a .env.example with no real values, and load production secrets from a manager or platform environment injection.
entries.test_step:
1. Is .env tracked right now?
   $ git ls-files | grep -E '(^|/)\\.env$'
   Output means it is tracked.

2. Was it EVER committed? This is the question that decides whether secrets leaked:
   $ git log --all --oneline -- .env
   Any commit here means the values in it are public. Untracking will not change that.

3. If step 2 found anything, rotate every credential in the file now. Do this before
   the git work, not after.

4. Stop tracking it and ignore it:
   $ git rm --cached .env
   $ echo ".env" >> .gitignore
   $ git commit -m "Stop tracking .env" && git push

5. Verify what you actually achieved. This confirms the file is no longer tracked:
   $ git ls-files | grep -E '(^|/)\\.env$'   (should output nothing)
   It does NOT confirm the secret is gone. To check that, re-run step 2. It will
   still list the old commits. Only a git-filter-repo rewrite plus a force push
   changes that, and clones and forks may keep copies regardless.

entries.title: Missing composer.lock: commit it for a project, skip it for a library
entries.summary: composer.lock pins the exact dependency versions a build resolved. For an application - a site, a deployed plugin, anything you install rather than require - commit it: Composer says doing so "will cause anyone who sets up the project to use the exact same versions of the dependencies that you are using". For a library, Composer is equally explicit that it is not necessary, because the lock file is ignored when the package is installed as a dependency and would only pin versions for your own contributors. Without a committed lock file in a project, versions are not random: composer install resolves the constraints in composer.json afresh, so two installs at different times produce different builds from identical source, and the difference surfaces wherever the newer release changed behaviour.
entries.test_step:
1. First decide which one this is. Open composer.json and read "type": a library that
   others require does not need a committed lock file, and Composer says so. Everything
   you deploy or install - a site, a plugin, a theme - is a project, and does.

2. For a project, check whether composer.json is tracked and composer.lock is not:
   $ git ls-files | grep composer.json
   $ git ls-files | grep composer.lock
   
   composer.json present AND composer.lock absent -> RISK.

3. If missing, generate the lock file locally:
   $ composer install
   $ git add composer.lock
   $ git commit -m "Add composer.lock for reproducible builds"
   $ git push

4. Verify lock file presence in remote:
   $ git ls-files | grep composer.lock
   (Should output: composer.lock)

5. Confirm .gitignore does NOT exclude composer.lock:
   $ grep "^composer.lock" .gitignore
   (Should return nothing; lock file is tracked.)

6. Test determinism across environments:
   $ git clone <repo>
   $ cd <repo>
   $ composer install
   $ vendor/bin/phpunit  // Uses exact versions from lock file

entries.title: Hardcoded API keys and secrets in code expose credentials: move to environment variables
entries.summary: Never hardcode API keys, database passwords, license keys, or OAuth tokens in PHP code. These credentials are readable in git history, backups, logs, and error messages, exposing accounts and data to anyone with repo access. Load them from environment variables, a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, 1Password), or a git-ignored .env read via php-dotenv. wp-config.php is the exception rather than a violation: WordPress puts DB_PASSWORD and the salts there by design, and the official hardening guide protects the file by location and permissions rather than by moving the values out - it may sit one directory above the web root, should be readable only by you and the web server (400 or 440), and can be denied outright in .htaccess. What must never happen is a credential in a file that ships to the repository or to a client. Strip hardcoded credentials immediately and rotate all exposed accounts.
entries.test_step:
1. Search for common secret patterns in code (hardcoded keys):
   $ grep -r "sk_live\|sk_test\|ghp_\|STRIPE_SECRET\|API_KEY\s*=" \
     --include="*.php" src/ plugins/ wp-content/
   
   Flag any matches that are NOT variable assignments from $_ENV or environment lookups.

2. Check git history for accidentally committed secrets:
   $ git log --all --oneline -S 'sk_live' -- '*.php'
   $ git log --all --oneline -S 'DATABASE_PASSWORD' -- '*.php'
   
   If output shows commits: secrets may have been exposed.

3. If hardcoded secrets found:
   a. Identify the account/service (Stripe, SendGrid, GitHub, etc.)
   b. Rotate the secret immediately (generate new key, disable old one)
   c. Move secret to .env (or production secrets manager)
   d. Remove hardcoded secret from code
   e. Commit and push

4. Verify no hardcoded secrets remain:
   $ grep -r "sk_live\|api_key\s*=\s*['\"]" --include="*.php" src/ plugins/
   (Should return no matches, or only matches from environment lookups.)

5. For each secret that was rotated:
   - Stripe: Revoke old key in Dashboard → API Keys
   - SendGrid: Revoke in Settings → API Keys
   - GitHub: Revoke in Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens
   - Database: Change password in DB admin panel; update .env

entries.title: $wpdb queries must use $wpdb->prepare(): direct variable interpolation is SQL injection
entries.summary: Passing PHP variables directly into $wpdb query methods (get_results, query, get_var, get_row) via string interpolation or concatenation creates SQL injection vulnerabilities. Always use $wpdb->prepare() with %d/%s/%f placeholders to parameterise the query. WordPress will throw a doing_it_wrong() notice on unprepared queries in WP 3.6+.
entries.test_step:
1. Enable WP_DEBUG = true and WP_DEBUG_LOG = true in wp-config.php.
2. Search plugin/theme code for calls to $wpdb->query, $wpdb->get_results, $wpdb->get_var, $wpdb->get_row, $wpdb->get_col.
3. For each call, check whether the argument is $wpdb->prepare(...). If not, flag it.
4. Replace direct variable interpolation with $wpdb->prepare() placeholders (%d, %s, %f).
5. Check debug.log for "Unprepared queries" or "doing_it_wrong" notices after saving.

entries.title: register_rest_route() without permission_callback exposes the endpoint to unauthenticated requests
entries.summary: Since WordPress 5.5, every REST route must declare a permission_callback. Omitting it causes a doing_it_wrong() notice and defaults to no permission check. Anyone can call the endpoint. For public read-only routes use __return_true explicitly and document why. For mutating routes (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) or routes that return private data, always check current_user_can() inside the callback.
entries.test_step:
1. Search plugin/theme code for register_rest_route( calls. Do this by hand even if an automatic check reported nothing: pattern matching can only judge a registration whose arguments are written out in the call itself. Where the arguments are assembled in a variable beforehand, or include an anonymous function, the automatic check stays silent and says nothing about the route either way.
2. For each registration, verify the options array contains a permission_callback key.
3. If permission_callback is __return_true, confirm the route only reads public data. Flag it if it mutates state or returns private content.
4. Test with WP_DEBUG = true: a missing permission_callback emits a doing_it_wrong() notice in WP 5.5+.
5. For mutating routes, test that unauthenticated requests receive a 401/403 REST error.

entries.title: AJAX and form handlers must verify a nonce. Missing wp_verify_nonce() / check_ajax_referer() enables CSRF
entries.summary: WordPress AJAX handlers (wp_ajax_{action} / wp_ajax_nopriv_{action}) and admin-post.php form handlers that mutate state without verifying a nonce are vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). An attacker can trick an authenticated user's browser into triggering the action on their behalf. Always call wp_verify_nonce() or check_ajax_referer() at the top of any handler that performs a write operation.
entries.test_step:
1. Find all add_action( 'wp_ajax_' and add_action( 'wp_ajax_nopriv_' registrations in the codebase.
2. Open each handler function and check for a check_ajax_referer() or wp_verify_nonce() call at the top.
3. If missing, add wp_create_nonce( 'action_name' ) in the localize/form output and check_ajax_referer( 'action_name', 'nonce_field' ) at the handler start.
4. Test: send an AJAX request without the nonce field. It should fail with a -1 or wp_die() response.
5. Test: send a valid request with the correct nonce. It should succeed.

entries.title: $_POST / $_GET / $_REQUEST values must be sanitised with a sanitize_*() function before use
entries.summary: Every value read from $_POST, $_GET, or $_REQUEST is user-controlled and must be sanitised before being used in database queries, option updates, file operations, or any logic that affects system state. WordPress provides context-specific sanitise functions: sanitize_text_field(), sanitize_email(), sanitize_url(), absint(), wp_kses() etc. Using raw superglobals without sanitisation exposes the code to stored XSS, SQL injection (when $wpdb->prepare() is also missing), and arbitrary data corruption.
entries.bad_pattern:
// WRONG, raw superglobal assigned without sanitisation.
$username = $_POST['username'];      // Could be anything; used in queries below.
$post_id  = $_GET['id'];             // String; not cast to int.
$message  = $_REQUEST['message'];    // Used unfiltered in update_option().

// These then get passed downstream:
update_option( 'my_plugin_username', $username );   // Stores arbitrary input.
$wpdb->get_results( "SELECT * FROM ... WHERE id = $post_id" ); // SQL injection.
entries.test_step:
1. Search for $var = $_POST[ / $var = $_GET[ / $var = $_REQUEST[ assignments.
2. For each, trace $var to its first use. Check whether it passes through a sanitize_*() function or a type cast before use.
3. For numeric IDs: wrap with absint().
4. For text: wrap with sanitize_text_field( wp_unslash( ... ) ).
5. Verify: attempt to submit a value containing <script>alert(1)</script> via the affected field. Confirm it is stripped before storage or output.

entries.title: Admin and mutating actions must check current_user_can() before executing privileged operations
entries.summary: Any action that creates, updates, or deletes data. Whether triggered via wp_ajax_, admin_post_, admin_action_, or a direct page callback. Must verify the current user holds the required capability with current_user_can() before executing. Without this check, any logged-in (or even logged-out, for nopriv routes) user can trigger the operation regardless of their role. Combine with nonce verification: the nonce proves the request is intentional; the capability check proves the user is authorised.
entries.test_step:
1. Find all add_action( 'wp_ajax_', add_action( 'admin_post_', and add_action( 'admin_action_' registrations.
2. Open each handler and confirm a current_user_can() call appears before any write operation.
3. Test: log in as a Subscriber, send a crafted POST to admin-ajax.php?action={your_action} or admin-post.php?action={your_action}.
4. Without the capability check, the operation succeeds. With it, the user receives a wp_die() or error response.
5. Also verify: the nonce check comes BEFORE the capability check (fail fast, avoid timing attacks).

entries.title: the_content filter callbacks need an is_main_query() + in_the_loop() guard to avoid firing in admin, feeds, and secondary queries
entries.summary: The the_content filter fires in many contexts: the main loop, secondary WP_Query loops, REST API responses, widget areas, feeds (RSS/Atom), and wp-admin. A callback that always modifies content will inject unwanted output in feeds, duplicate content in pages with multiple queries, and corrupt admin editor previews. Guard with in_the_loop() && is_main_query() (or with a more specific condition (is_singular(), !is_admin(), !is_feed())) so the modification only runs where it is intended.
entries.test_step:
1. Find all add_filter( 'the_content', ... ) registrations in the codebase.
2. Open each callback and check whether it returns $content unchanged when in_the_loop() is false or is_main_query() is false.
3. Test on a page that has a secondary WP_Query (e.g. a related-posts widget) (verify the callback does not fire twice.
4. Test the RSS feed (/feed/)) verify the extra content does not appear in the feed if that is not intended.
5. Test in wp-admin post preview. Verify no corruption appears.

entries.title: useSetting() hook deprecated in WP 6.5: migrate to useSettings()
entries.summary: The useSetting() hook was deprecated in WordPress 6.5.0 in favor of useSettings(). useSettings() provides better performance by retrieving multiple settings in a single call, while useSetting() remains a backward-compatibility wrapper. Existing code calling useSetting() will still work but should migrate.
entries.test_step: In a block's edit.tsx/jsx, replace useSetting() calls with useSettings(), passing multiple setting keys. Verify in the browser DevTools console (WP 6.5+) that no deprecation warnings appear.

entries.title: wp.blocks.isValidBlockContent() removed: use validateBlock() instead
entries.summary: The wp.blocks.isValidBlockContent() function was removed because it ignores innerBlocks when validating, leading to incorrect results. Use wp.blocks.validateBlock() instead, which accepts the full block object and validates correctly. Any code relying on isValidBlockContent() will fail silently or throw errors on affected WordPress versions.
entries.test_step: Search block validation code for isValidBlockContent( calls. Replace with validateBlock(), passing the full block object (name, attributes, innerBlocks). Test that validation respects innerBlock content.

entries.title: Block API version 2 deprecated in WP 6.9: migrate to apiVersion 3
entries.summary: Starting in WordPress 6.9, blocks registered with apiVersion 2 or lower trigger browser console warnings. Gutenberg 23.6 and WordPress 7.1 always iframe the Post Editor regardless of apiVersion (Block Editor handbook migration guide), so v1/v2 no longer opts a post out of the iframe. useBlockProps() is not what version 3 adds: the Block API docs make it a version 2 requirement for the edit implementation, so a correct v2 block already calls it. What version 3 signals is iframe readiness: do not reach for the parent document/window, and load canvas editor styles via editorStyle. See wp-7-1-post-editor-always-iframe and wp-7-1-post-editor-iframe-owner-document.
entries.test_step: Open block.json or registerBlockType() calls. Check browser console in WP 6.9+ for apiVersion warnings. Verify useBlockProps() is used in both edit and save functions. Test block rendering in iframe editor (WP 7.1+).

entries.title: Global functions, classes, hooks, and options must use a unique plugin prefix to prevent naming collisions
entries.summary: WordPress Plugin Check (Prefixing_Check) requires every globally accessible symbol. Functions, classes, interfaces, traits, namespaces, global variables, options, and transients. To be prefixed with a unique, plugin-specific identifier. The official rule: at least 4 characters, not a common English word, and not a reserved WP prefix (wp_, __, _). Missing prefixes cause silent naming collisions when two plugins define the same global symbol, producing fatal "Cannot redeclare" errors or silently overwriting each other's options. PHP namespaces are the modern alternative: they satisfy the requirement without prefixing every symbol name.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: namespace isolates all class/function symbols.
namespace Acme\MyPlugin;

class Settings_Page {
    public function register(): void {
        add_action( 'admin_menu', [ $this, 'add_page' ] );
    }
    public function add_page(): void {
        add_options_page( 'Acme Settings', 'Acme', 'manage_options', 'acme-settings', [ $this, 'render' ] );
    }
}

// CORRECT: option key prefixed even inside a namespace.
update_option( 'acme_myplugin_version', '1.0.0' );

// CORRECT: global function with unique prefix (when not using namespaces).
function acme_get_settings(): array {
    return (array) get_option( 'acme_myplugin_settings', [] );
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: global functions without a prefix. Fatal "Cannot redeclare" if another
// plugin defines the same function name.
function save_post_data(): void { ... }
function get_settings(): array { ... }

// WRONG: class name that will collide with other plugins named "Admin".
class Admin { ... }

// WRONG: unprefixed option key; any plugin reading 'settings' will get your data.
update_option( 'settings', $my_settings );

// WRONG: custom hook tag without a prefix; fires on every add_action( 'init'.. ).
do_action( 'init_plugin' );
entries.test_step:
1. Run Plugin Check (free plugin from wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-check) on your plugin.
2. Alternatively, run PHPCS: phpcs --standard=WordPress --sniffs=WordPress.NamingConventions.PrefixAllGlobals --runtime-set prefixes myplugin /path/to/plugin.
3. Review every reported symbol. Function, class, constant, option name.
4. Either add a unique plugin prefix to each global symbol, or wrap your code in a PHP namespace.
5. Re-run the check. No PrefixAllGlobals warnings should remain.

entries.title: PHP plugin files must include the ABSPATH direct-access guard to prevent execution when loaded directly
entries.summary: WordPress Plugin Check (Direct_File_Access_Check, since 1.8.0) flags PHP plugin files that contain procedural code or function calls but lack a guard against direct HTTP access. Without the `if ( ! defined( 'ABSPATH' ) ) { exit; }` check, a file loaded directly via a browser URL executes outside WordPress's bootstrap. Exposing early-stage code to uninitialized globals, missing security filters, and potential information disclosure. Files that consist solely of a class declaration are exempt (no procedural execution risk).
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: guard is the very first statement after the opening tag.
if ( ! defined( 'ABSPATH' ) ) {
    exit; // Exit if accessed directly.
}

// Everything below runs only when WordPress is loaded.
function acme_register_post_type(): void {
    register_post_type( 'acme_product', [
        'public' => true,
        'label'  => 'Products',
    ] );
}
add_action( 'init', 'acme_register_post_type' );
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: no ABSPATH guard. Requesting /wp-content/plugins/myplugin/helpers.php
// directly executes the following code outside WordPress.

require_once plugin_dir_path( __FILE__ ) . 'config.php'; // fatal: plugin_dir_path undefined
global $wpdb; // $wpdb is null, queries will error
$data = $wpdb->get_results( "SELECT * FROM wp_options LIMIT 5" );
entries.test_step:
1. Run Plugin Check on your plugin. Direct_File_Access_Check fires on each PHP file missing the ABSPATH guard.
2. Manually: open every PHP file in your plugin that is not a pure class file.
3. Confirm the first executable statement after <?php is: if ( ! defined( 'ABSPATH' ) ) { exit; }
4. Add the guard to any file that lacks it.
5. Verify: curl -I https://yoursite.com/wp-content/plugins/myplugin/your-file.php. The response should be an empty body (exit fires) rather than PHP output or a fatal error message.

entries.title: i18n functions (__(), _e(), esc_html__() etc.) must include the plugin's text-domain. Omitting it breaks translations
entries.summary: WordPress Plugin Check (I18n_Usage_Check) uses the WordPress.WP.I18n PHPCS sniff to require a correct, hardcoded text-domain string as the last argument to every i18n function: __(), _e(), _n(), _x(), esc_html__(), esc_attr__(), esc_html_e(), esc_attr_e(). Omitting the domain makes the string untranslatable. It falls through to the 'default' domain and will never be loaded from the plugin's language files. Using a dynamic variable as the domain (NonSingularStringLiteralDomain) also fails the check because WordPress loads language files at boot time based on a static domain string.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: text-domain matches the plugin slug and Plugin Header.
// Plugin header: Text Domain: acme-forms

__( 'Form submitted successfully.', 'acme-forms' )
_e( 'Save settings', 'acme-forms' )
_n( 'One entry', '%d entries', $count, 'acme-forms' )
esc_html__( 'Error saving data.', 'acme-forms' )
esc_attr__( 'Search forms', 'acme-forms' )

// CORRECT: translated strings in a class method.
class Acme_Forms_Admin {
    public function get_notice(): string {
        return esc_html__( 'Settings saved.', 'acme-forms' );
    }
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG, no text-domain: string falls through to core 'default' domain.
// Plugin Check: WordPress.WP.I18n.MissingArgDomain
__( 'Form submitted successfully.' )
_e( 'Save settings' )
esc_html__( 'Error saving data.' )

// WRONG, dynamic domain: cannot be resolved at load time.
// Plugin Check: WordPress.WP.I18n.NonSingularStringLiteralDomain
$domain = 'acme-forms';
__( 'Settings', $domain )

// WRONG, wrong domain: string will not match the plugin's .po file.
__( 'Submit', 'some-other-plugin' )
entries.test_step:
1. Run Plugin Check on your plugin. I18n_Usage_Check reports every missing or wrong text-domain.
2. Alternatively: phpcs --standard=WordPress --sniffs=WordPress.WP.I18n --runtime-set text_domain your-plugin-slug /path/to/plugin.
3. For each MissingArgDomain error, add your plugin slug as the final argument.
4. For NonSingularStringLiteralDomain warnings, replace the variable with a string literal.
5. Verify translations load: install Loco Translate or WP CLI (wp i18n make-pot) and confirm the strings appear in the generated .pot file.

entries.title: wp_enqueue_script() and wp_enqueue_style() must be scoped: loading assets on every page wastes bandwidth and hurts Core Web Vitals
entries.summary: WordPress Plugin Check (Enqueued_Scripts_Scope_Check, since 1.0.2) is a runtime check that visits multiple URL types and flags any plugin script or stylesheet that loads on EVERY page. Including the homepage, archives, and post types that do not use the feature. Unconditional enqueuing increases page weight for all visitors, hurts Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and Total Blocking Time (TBT), The check reports this as a warning, which is a review finding rather than evidence of rejection - we have no data on how often it decides a submission, and this entry does not claim any. Scope every asset to the pages or post types that actually need it.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: enqueue scoped to single product pages only.
add_action( 'wp_enqueue_scripts', 'acme_enqueue_product_assets' );

function acme_enqueue_product_assets(): void {
    // Gate: only load on pages that actually render this feature.
    if ( ! is_singular( 'product' ) ) {
        return;
    }
    wp_enqueue_script(
        'acme-product-gallery',
        plugin_dir_url( __FILE__ ) . 'assets/gallery.js',
        [ 'jquery' ],
        '1.0.0',
        true // load in footer
    );
    wp_enqueue_style(
        'acme-product-gallery',
        plugin_dir_url( __FILE__ ) . 'assets/gallery.css',
        [],
        '1.0.0'
    );
}

// CORRECT: shortcode detection (load only when the shortcode is on the page).
add_action( 'wp_enqueue_scripts', 'acme_maybe_enqueue_form_assets' );

function acme_maybe_enqueue_form_assets(): void {
    global $post;
    if ( ! is_a( $post, 'WP_Post' ) || ! has_shortcode( $post->post_content, 'acme_form' ) ) {
        return;
    }
    wp_enqueue_script( 'acme-form', plugin_dir_url( __FILE__ ) . 'assets/form.js', [], '1.0.0', true );
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: loads on every front-end page, regardless of whether the feature is used.
add_action( 'wp_enqueue_scripts', 'acme_enqueue_all_assets' );

function acme_enqueue_all_assets(): void {
    // No conditional, 200 KB script loads on the homepage, archives, search, etc.
    wp_enqueue_script(
        'acme-product-gallery',
        plugin_dir_url( __FILE__ ) . 'assets/gallery.js',
        [ 'jquery' ],
        '1.0.0',
        true
    );
    wp_enqueue_style(
        'acme-product-gallery',
        plugin_dir_url( __FILE__ ) . 'assets/gallery.css',
        [],
        '1.0.0'
    );
}
entries.test_step:
1. Run Plugin Check. Enqueued_Scripts_Scope_Check loads several page types, among them the homepage, a single post and an archive, and flags any script or style present in all of them. Read the list it visited from the run rather than assuming these three.
2. Manually: open your browser's network panel on the homepage and check whether plugin scripts are loaded even though the plugin feature is not visible.
3. Wrap every wp_enqueue_script() / wp_enqueue_style() in a conditional: if ( is_singular( 'post' ) ) { ... } or equivalent.
4. Re-run Plugin Check. No scope warnings should remain for your plugin handle.
5. Verify: the asset is absent on the homepage (devtools → Network → filter by your script handle).

entries.title: Use wp_safe_redirect() instead of wp_redirect() when the URL may be user-controlled: open redirect vulnerability
entries.summary: WordPress Plugin Check (Safe_Redirect_Check, since 1.7.0) flags wp_redirect() calls and recommends wp_safe_redirect() as a security best practice. The critical vulnerability: when the URL passed to wp_redirect() originates from $_GET['redirect_to'] or similar user-controlled input without validation, an attacker can craft a link to your plugin page with a redirect_to pointing to a phishing domain. Authenticated users who click the link get silently redirected. wp_safe_redirect() restricts the destination to the same host and an explicit allowlist (filtered by allowed_redirect_hosts), making open-redirect attacks impossible by default.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: wp_safe_redirect() restricts destination to same-host or allowlist.
add_action( 'admin_post_acme_handle_form', 'acme_handle_form' );

function acme_handle_form(): void {
    check_admin_referer( 'acme_form_nonce', 'security' );

    if ( ! current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) ) {
        wp_die( esc_html__( 'Not allowed.', 'acme' ) );
    }

    // User-supplied redirect_to is safe, wp_safe_redirect validates the host.
    $redirect_to = isset( $_POST['redirect_to'] )
        ? esc_url_raw( wp_unslash( $_POST['redirect_to'] ) )
        : '';

    wp_safe_redirect( $redirect_to ?: admin_url( 'admin.php?page=acme-settings&saved=1' ) );
    exit; // Always exit after redirect.
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: wp_redirect() with user-controlled URL is an open redirect.
// Attacker crafts: /wp-admin/admin-post.php?action=acme_handle_form&redirect_to=https://evil.com
add_action( 'admin_post_acme_handle_form', 'acme_handle_form' );

function acme_handle_form(): void {
    // esc_url_raw validates format but does NOT restrict the host.
    $redirect_to = esc_url_raw( $_GET['redirect_to'] ?? admin_url() );
    wp_redirect( $redirect_to ); // Open redirect: any external URL works.
    // Missing exit, page renders anyway even when redirect fires.
}
entries.test_step:
1. Run Plugin Check. Safe_Redirect_Check flags every wp_redirect() call.
2. Search your codebase for wp_redirect(: grep -r 'wp_redirect(' /path/to/plugin.
3. For each hit, check whether the URL argument could come from $_GET, $_POST, or any user-controlled variable.
4. Replace wp_redirect() with wp_safe_redirect(). The function signature is identical.
5. Ensure exit; follows immediately after wp_safe_redirect().
6. Test: craft a URL with redirect_to=https://evil.com and confirm wp_safe_redirect() sends the user to admin_url() instead (fallback behavior when host is not allowed).

entries.title: register_setting() must include a sanitize_callback: missing sanitisation stores raw user input in wp_options
entries.summary: WordPress Plugin Check (Setting_Sanitization_Check, since 1.4.0) flags register_setting() calls that omit a sanitize_callback or provide an invalid one (empty string, false). Without sanitisation, WordPress stores the raw $_POST value directly in the wp_options table when the Settings API processes a form submission. An attacker with settings-page access (subscriber with custom capabilities, or after exploiting a CSRF gap) can store arbitrary data including XSS payloads that fire when an admin later views the settings page. The sanitize_callback is the last defense before persistence.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: sanitize_callback provided for each registered setting.
add_action( 'admin_init', 'acme_register_settings' );

function acme_register_settings(): void {
    register_setting(
        'acme_options_group',
        'acme_api_key',
        [
            'type'              => 'string',
            'sanitize_callback' => 'sanitize_text_field',
            'default'           => '',
            'show_in_rest'      => false,
        ]
    );

    register_setting(
        'acme_options_group',
        'acme_max_results',
        [
            'type'              => 'integer',
            'sanitize_callback' => 'absint',
            'default'           => 10,
        ]
    );
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: no sanitize_callback; raw $_POST is stored in wp_options.
// Plugin Check: PluginCheck.CodeAnalysis.SettingSanitization.register_settingMissing
add_action( 'admin_init', 'acme_register_settings' );

function acme_register_settings(): void {
    register_setting( 'acme_options_group', 'acme_api_key' );
    register_setting( 'acme_options_group', 'acme_max_results' );
}

// WRONG: invalid callback (empty string).
// Plugin Check: PluginCheck.CodeAnalysis.SettingSanitization.register_settingInvalid
register_setting( 'acme_options_group', 'acme_setting', [
    'sanitize_callback' => '',
] );
entries.test_step:
1. Run Plugin Check. Setting_Sanitization_Check flags every register_setting() missing a valid sanitize_callback with severity 7.
2. Search your codebase: grep -r 'register_setting(' /path/to/plugin.
3. For each call, confirm the $args array contains a valid, callable 'sanitize_callback'.
4. Add the appropriate sanitise function (sanitize_text_field, absint, sanitize_email, or a custom function) to each registration.
5. Test: submit a settings form with a payload containing <script>alert(1)</script> in a text field. Verify the stored value in wp_options is stripped of the tag.

entries.title: WordPress Abilities API: register with meta.mcp.public to expose to MCP clients
entries.summary: WordPress abilities registered with wp_register_ability() are NOT visible to MCP clients (Claude Code, Cursor, agent tools) by default. The ability works inside the WordPress admin and is discoverable via REST, but MCP clients cannot see it without an explicit opt-in. Added in the WordPress MCP Adapter (February 2026. After every major model's training cutoff), abilities require 'meta' => ['mcp' => ['public' => true]] to appear in MCP discovery. The two visibility layers are independent: show_in_rest controls the REST API; mcp.public controls the MCP server.
entries.test_step:
1. Register the ability without meta.mcp.public (bad pattern above).
2. Start the MCP Adapter server: HTTP at /wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server or STDIO via `wp mcp-adapter serve`.
3. Run the mcp-adapter-discover-abilities tool. Confirm the ability does NOT appear.
4. Add 'mcp' => ['public' => true] to the meta array (correct pattern above).
5. Restart the server, run discovery again. The ability now appears in results.

entries.title: WordPress 7.0: use watch() from @wordpress/interactivity, not effect from @preact/signals
entries.summary: WordPress 7.0 (May 20, 2026. After your model's training cutoff) added watch() as the public reactive-callback API in @wordpress/interactivity. watch() is exported as an alias for @preact/signals's effect(), but effect itself was never a named export from @wordpress/interactivity. Code that imports effect directly from @preact/signals, or that expects import { effect } from "@wordpress/interactivity" to resolve, will throw a module resolution error or silently use a stale signals version. Always import watch from @wordpress/interactivity.
entries.test_step: In your interactivity store JS, replace any direct @preact/signals effect() import with import { watch } from "@wordpress/interactivity". Verify no "effect is not exported" module errors appear in the browser console on WP 7.0+. Run `npm run build` and confirm no unresolved dependency warnings for @preact/signals.

entries.title: WordPress Abilities API: mutating ability with __return_true permission_callback is a privilege escalation
entries.summary: A WordPress ability registered with `permission_callback => '__return_true'` (or `fn() => true`) grants any authenticated MCP user permission to execute it, regardless of what it modifies. The MCP Adapter's execute-ability meta-tool calls `$ability->check_permissions()` before executing. This callback IS the only application-level gate. On a read-only ability this is often acceptable; on a mutating ability (creating posts, updating options, modifying users) it is a privilege escalation: any subscriber-level user on the site who can reach the MCP endpoint can execute the operation.
entries.test_step:
1. Register the ability with 'permission_callback' => '__return_true' (bad pattern above).
2. Create a subscriber-level WordPress user (no publish_posts capability).
3. Authenticate as that subscriber on the MCP server endpoint.
4. Call mcp-adapter-execute-ability with ability_name = 'my-plugin/publish-all-drafts'. It succeeds. All drafts are published.
5. Restore permission_callback to fn() => current_user_can('publish_posts') (correct pattern).
6. Repeat step 4. The execute-ability call now returns a permission error.

entries.title: WordPress 7.0: state.navigation.hasStarted / hasFinished deprecated in core/router
entries.summary: WordPress 7.0 (May 20, 2026. After your model's training cutoff) deprecated the state.navigation.hasStarted and state.navigation.hasFinished properties in the @wordpress/interactivity-router (core/router) store. These were always internal implementation details and now trigger a console warning in development mode (when SCRIPT_DEBUG is enabled) when accessed. They will stop working in WordPress 7.1. The official replacement mechanism for tracking navigation state is planned for WP 7.1. Until then, avoid reading these properties.
entries.test_step: Search your interactivity JS for state.navigation.hasStarted or state.navigation.hasFinished. If found, open the browser console in WP 7.0. You should see a deprecation warning. Remove the reads and manage loading state locally. Verify no warnings appear after the change.

entries.title: WordPress Abilities API: ability with no declared input_schema properties receives unvalidated MCP input
entries.summary: An ability registered with an empty `input_schema` (no `properties` declared, or the schema is omitted entirely) receives the raw MCP client input in `execute_callback` without field-level validation. The WordPress Abilities API validates inputs only against declared schema properties. With no properties declared, any field the MCP client sends passes through. Including unexpected keys. This is a correctness issue on read-only abilities (wrong fields silently ignored) and a security issue on mutating abilities (injected parameters may alter execution path).
entries.test_step:
1. Register the ability with empty input_schema (bad pattern above).
2. Call mcp-adapter-execute-ability with ability_name = 'my-plugin/delete-post' and parameters = {post_id: 'DROP TABLE wp_posts;--'}. The callback receives the raw string as post_id and attempts wp_delete_post() with it (casted to 0 by PHP, deleting nothing, but no error thrown either).
3. Call again with parameters = {} (missing post_id). $input['post_id'] is null; callback still runs without error.
4. Add the correct input_schema with 'post_id' declared as integer (correct pattern above).
5. Repeat both bad calls. Abilities API now rejects them before the callback runs.

entries.title: WordPress 7.0 requires PHP 7.4+: PHP 7.2 and 7.3 no longer supported
entries.summary: WordPress 7.0 (May 20, 2026. After your model's training cutoff) raised the minimum supported PHP version to 7.4. PHP 7.2 and 7.3 are no longer tested or supported. Any plugin or theme that declares "Requires PHP: 7.2" or "Requires PHP: 7.3" in its headers, or targets PHP 7.2/7.3 syntax in its CI matrix, is now running below the WordPress minimum. Update the Requires PHP header, composer.json platform constraint, and CI matrix to PHP 7.4+.
entries.test_step: Check your plugin/theme file header for "Requires PHP". If it says 7.2 or 7.3, update to 7.4. Update composer.json require.php and config.platform.php. Update your CI PHP matrix to start at 7.4. Run composer check-platform-reqs to verify no typed-property or arrow-function syntax is guarded behind PHP_VERSION_ID checks targeting 7.2/7.3.

entries.title: WordPress Abilities API: ability with no permission_callback has no access gate for MCP execution
entries.summary: A `wp_register_ability()` call without a `permission_callback` key leaves the ability's access gate undefined. The MCP Adapter's execute-ability path calls `$ability->check_permissions()` before executing, without a callback this falls back to whatever the WordPress Abilities API's `WP_Ability` class does with a missing callback. The `creating-abilities.md` guide in the official repo lists `permission_callback` as a structural requirement. Omitting it on any ability exposed via `mcp.public: true` is a security gap; on a mutating ability it is critical.
entries.test_step:
1. Register the ability without permission_callback (bad pattern above).
2. Create a subscriber-level user and authenticate as that user on the MCP server.
3. Call mcp-adapter-execute-ability with ability_name = 'my-plugin/reset-settings' and parameters = {}. Observe the result (expect execute to proceed if no callback gate blocks it).
4. Add the correct permission_callback returning current_user_can('manage_options').
5. Repeat step 3. Expect a permission error for the subscriber.

entries.title: WordPress Abilities API: ability with type:resource is silently dropped if meta.uri is absent
entries.summary: An ability registered with `'mcp' => ['type' => 'resource']` but without a `'uri'` key at `meta.mcp.uri` will be silently dropped when the MCP Adapter's default server auto-discovers resources. `DefaultServerFactory::discover_abilities_by_type('resource')` collects the ability name, but `RegisterAbilityAsMcpResource::build()` calls `get_uri()` which returns `WP_Error('resource_uri_not_found', ...)` when the URI is absent. The ability is dropped from the MCP server's resource list without any visible PHP error to the developer. Setting `uri` at the top-level `meta['uri']` (instead of `meta['mcp']['uri']`) still works as a deprecated fallback but triggers a `_doing_it_wrong` notice since 0.5.0.
entries.test_step:
1. Register the ability without 'uri' at meta.mcp.uri (bad pattern above).
2. Start the MCP Adapter default server and call mcp-adapter-discover-abilities. The ability does not appear in the resource list.
3. Inspect the WordPress error log. Look for a WP_Error with code 'resource_uri_not_found' from RegisterAbilityAsMcpResource::get_uri().
4. Add 'uri' => 'wordpress://my-plugin/site-config' inside the 'mcp' key (correct pattern above).
5. Restart and call the relevant MCP resource listing. The resource now appears.

entries.title: SCF includes gallery, repeater, flexible content, and clone: they are not Pro-only
entries.summary: Secure Custom Fields (SCF). The WordPress-maintained fork of ACF bundled in WordPress.org plugin recommendations. Includes the gallery, repeater, flexible content, and clone field types. These were historically ACF Pro-only features. On any site running SCF, they are available without a paid license. Code that gates these fields behind an ACF Pro version check (e.g., checking acf_get_setting("pro") or the ACF_PRO constant) will have a permanently false branch on SCF-powered sites. Verify which plugin is active before assuming these fields require a paid upgrade.
entries.test_step: On a site running Secure Custom Fields (not ACF Pro), register a gallery or repeater field and confirm it renders without a Pro license. Search your codebase for ACF_PRO, acf_is_pro(), or acf()->pro checks gating gallery/repeater/flexible-content usage. Remove the gate if the only intent was to check field-type availability.

entries.title: block.json scaffold: minimal, spec-compliant block registration template
entries.summary: A block.json skeleton for WordPress 6.3 and later. Only two fields are actually required by the Block API - name and title - and everything else below is optional; they are shown because a real block wants most of them, not because registration fails without them. category must be one of the six core categories (text, media, design, widgets, theme, embed) or one you register yourself; a value core does not know silently drops the block into the fallback group. apiVersion 3 arrived in WordPress 6.3, so this scaffold does not fit an older floor. The $schema line is what gives an editor autocompletion. Copy it, rename the namespace and slug, and register with register_block_type_from_metadata().
entries.test_step: Validate block.json against its schema - your editor does this from the $schema line, and any JSON-schema validator does it in CI. `wp-scripts lint-js` will not: it lints JavaScript and TypeScript and never reads block.json. Then open the Block Editor and confirm the block appears in the inserter under the category you named; landing somewhere else means the category is not one core knows.

entries.title: WordPress production deploy checklist: 12 gates before you push
entries.summary: A 12-gate pre-deploy checklist for WordPress agency projects. Covers backups, database migration, cache warming, HTTP redirects, PHP error log, and smoke tests. Run this before every production push, not just major releases.
entries.code_example:
# Quick smoke via WP-CLI
wp option get siteurl
wp option get home
wp db check
wp cache flush
wp cron event list
wp plugin list --status=inactive  # confirm nothing unintentionally deactivated
entries.bad_pattern:
# Common anti-patterns
wp db export > backup.sql && rsync -av . user@prod:/var/www/html  # no restore test, no cache flush
wp plugin update --all --skip-plugins --skip-themes  # runs during traffic; no maintenance mode
entries.test_step: After deploy: open the site URL directly (no browser cache), log in to wp-admin, navigate to WooCommerce > Orders (if present), run `wp cron event run --due-now`, and tail `debug.log` for 60 s. Zero PHP errors = gate passed.

entries.title: REST API: register_rest_route must declare permission_callback: omitting it exposes the endpoint publicly
entries.summary: Every route registered via register_rest_route() must include a permission_callback that returns true (allowed) or a WP_Error (denied). Omitting the callback (or using '__return_true' on a mutating endpoint) makes the route publicly accessible to any unauthenticated caller. The callback fires before the main callback and is the sole authorization gate.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: gate to authenticated users with a capability
register_rest_route( 'my-plugin/v1', '/items', [
    'methods'  => 'GET',
    'callback' => 'get_private_items',
    'permission_callback' => function( $request ) {
        return current_user_can( 'read_private_posts' );
    },
] );

// CORRECT: public read is OK with __return_true; write is gated separately
register_rest_route( 'my-plugin/v1', '/items/(?P<id>\d+)', [
    [
        'methods'             => 'GET',
        'callback'            => 'get_item',
        'permission_callback' => '__return_true',
    ],
    [
        'methods'             => 'DELETE',
        'callback'            => 'delete_item',
        'permission_callback' => fn() => current_user_can( 'delete_posts' ),
    ],
] );
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: no permission_callback; endpoint is public to unauthenticated callers
register_rest_route( 'my-plugin/v1', '/items', [
    'methods'  => 'GET',
    'callback' => 'get_private_items',
] );

// WRONG: permission_callback always returns true on a mutating endpoint
register_rest_route( 'my-plugin/v1', '/items', [
    'methods'             => 'POST',
    'callback'            => 'create_item',
    'permission_callback' => '__return_true',
] );
entries.test_step: Register an endpoint without permission_callback. Make an unauthenticated HTTP GET request to /wp-json/my-plugin/v1/items and verify it returns 200 with data. This is the bug. Add permission_callback with a capability check. Repeat the unauthenticated request. It should now return 401 or 403.

entries.title: REST API: sanitize_callback alone skips schema validation: pair it with validate_callback
entries.summary: When you provide a custom sanitize_callback on a REST endpoint argument, WordPress skips its built-in JSON Schema validation for that argument. This means type, enum, and pattern constraints declared alongside sanitize_callback are silently ignored. An argument defined as enum: ['publish','draft','private'] accepts any string when sanitize_callback is set alone. Pair sanitize_callback with validate_callback (or use rest_validate_request_arg) to preserve schema enforcement.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: pair sanitize_callback with validate_callback (WP 5.3+)
register_rest_route( 'my-plugin/v1', '/post', [
    'methods'  => 'POST',
    'callback' => 'create_post',
    'args'     => [
        'status' => [
            'enum'              => [ 'publish', 'draft', 'private' ],
            'validate_callback' => 'rest_validate_request_arg',
            'sanitize_callback' => fn( $val ) => strtolower( $val ),
        ],
        'title' => [
            'type'              => 'string',
            'required'          => true,
            'validate_callback' => 'rest_validate_request_arg',
            'sanitize_callback' => 'sanitize_text_field',
        ],
    ],
] );
// Client sends: { "status": "INVALID" } → validate_callback rejects it → 400 Bad Request
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: sanitize_callback alone; enum constraint is not enforced
register_rest_route( 'my-plugin/v1', '/post', [
    'methods'  => 'POST',
    'callback' => 'create_post',
    'args'     => [
        'status' => [
            'enum'              => [ 'publish', 'draft', 'private' ],
            'sanitize_callback' => fn( $val ) => strtolower( $val ),
            // Missing: 'validate_callback'
            // Client sends: { "status": "INVALID" } → sanitizer lowercases it → "invalid" accepted
        ],
    ],
] );
entries.test_step: Register a REST arg with enum: ['publish','draft','private'] and sanitize_callback but no validate_callback. Send POST with {"status": "INVALID"}. Verify it is accepted (bypasses enum) (this is the bug. Add validate_callback => 'rest_validate_request_arg'. Repeat) should return 400 Bad Request.

entries.title: WordPress: checking $user->roles directly bypasses capability mapping: use current_user_can()
entries.summary: WordPress roles are collections of capabilities, not fixed identifiers. Checking in_array('administrator', \$user->roles) fails on multisite (where the role may differ), on custom role configurations, and when plugins rename or extend the role set. The correct pattern is current_user_can('capability') which resolves through the WP_Roles / WP_User::has_cap() system, respecting role-to-capability mappings, meta capability overrides, and plugin filters.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: capability check works across all role configurations
if ( current_user_can( 'delete_posts' ) ) {
    wp_delete_post( $post_id, true );
}

// Also correct: post-specific capability (checks authorship + global cap)
if ( current_user_can( 'delete_post', $post_id ) ) {
    wp_delete_post( $post_id, true );
}

// In admin menus, gate the page with a capability
add_submenu_page(
    'options-general.php',
    'My Settings',
    'My Settings',
    'manage_options',  // ← capability, not role name
    'my_settings',
    'render_my_settings_page'
);
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: checks role name, not capability; fails with custom roles
$user = get_user_by( 'ID', $user_id );
if ( in_array( 'administrator', $user->roles ) ) {
    wp_delete_post( $post_id, true );
}
// Fails if 'super_editor' has delete_posts cap but is not named 'administrator'
entries.test_step: Create a custom role 'editor_plus' with caps ['edit_posts','delete_posts']. Write code with in_array('administrator', \$user->roles). Assign 'editor_plus' to a test user. Verify deletion fails (wrong role name). This is the bug. Replace with current_user_can('delete_posts'). Verify deletion now works.

entries.title: WordPress: current_user_can() expects a capability, not a role name: use manage_options not administrator
entries.summary: current_user_can() expects a capability slug (manage_options, edit_posts, delete_posts), not a role name (administrator, editor). WordPress has a backward-compatibility fallback that treats role names as pseudo-capabilities on single sites, but it is unreliable on multisite and with custom role configurations. AI code frequently passes role names, producing code that silently fails in production configurations that differ from localhost.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: use capabilities, not role names
if ( current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) ) {
    update_option( 'site_settings', $settings );
}

if ( current_user_can( 'publish_posts' ) ) {
    wp_publish_post( $post_id );
}

if ( current_user_can( 'edit_others_posts' ) ) {
    // Grants access to editor AND administrator (and any role with that cap)
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: 'administrator' is a role name, not a capability
if ( current_user_can( 'administrator' ) ) {
    update_option( 'site_settings', $settings );
}

// WRONG: 'editor' is a role name
if ( current_user_can( 'editor' ) ) {
    wp_publish_post( $post_id );
}
entries.test_step: Create a custom role 'super_admin' with manage_options cap but not named 'administrator'. Write code: if (current_user_can('administrator')). Assign 'super_admin' to a test user. Verify check fails (role name mismatch). This is the bug. Replace with current_user_can('manage_options'). Verify check passes.

entries.title: WordPress: is_admin() checks the URL context, not user permissions: use current_user_can() for authorization
entries.summary: is_admin() returns true whenever the current request targets the wp-admin/ area. Including unauthenticated AJAX requests to wp-admin/admin-ajax.php. It does NOT check whether the current user has administrator privileges. Using is_admin() as a security gate allows any subscriber who triggers an admin-ajax.php request to pass the check and execute privileged code.
entries.code_example:
403 ] ); } } ); // CORRECT: combine for admin-only UI with security gate add_action( 'admin_notices', function() { if ( is_admin() && current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) ) { echo '

Admin notice.

'; } } ); // CORRECT: AJAX endpoint properly gated add_action( 'wp_ajax_my_action', function() { check_ajax_referer( 'my_nonce' ); if ( ! current_user_can( 'edit_posts' ) ) { wp_send_json_error( 'Insufficient permissions', 403 ); } wp_send_json_success( [ 'result' => 'ok' ] ); } );
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: is_admin() is not an authorization check
add_action( 'wp_loaded', function() {
    if ( is_admin() ) {
        // A subscriber with access to admin-ajax.php passes this check
        update_option( 'site_config', $_POST['config'] );
    }
} );
entries.test_step: Create a subscriber user. Write code: if ( is_admin() ) { update_option('secret', 'value'); }. Make an authenticated AJAX request from that subscriber to wp-admin/admin-ajax.php. Verify is_admin() returns true and option is updated (this is the bug. Replace with current_user_can('manage_options'). Repeat) option is not updated.

entries.title: WordPress: use wp_remote_get() / wp_remote_post() instead of raw curl_* or file_get_contents()
entries.summary: Raw curl_init() / curl_exec() calls inside WordPress code bypass the HTTP API (wp_remote_get, wp_remote_post). The WordPress HTTP API provides: unified timeout control, proxy/firewall compatibility, WP_Error on failure, SSL verification, and compatibility with object cache layers. curl_* gives you none of these. It also does not respect the WordPress 'http_api_transports' filter or the REQUESTS_SILENCE_PSR0_DEPRECATIONS constant. Use wp_remote_get() / wp_remote_post() for all HTTP requests inside WordPress.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: WordPress HTTP API with error handling
$response = wp_remote_get(
    'https://api.example.com/data',
    [ 'timeout' => 10 ]
);

if ( is_wp_error( $response ) ) {
    error_log( 'HTTP error: ' . $response->get_error_message() );
    return null;
}

$status = wp_remote_retrieve_response_code( $response );
if ( 200 !== $status ) {
    error_log( "API returned HTTP {$status}" );
    return null;
}

$body = wp_remote_retrieve_body( $response );
$data = json_decode( $body, true );

// For user-provided URLs (prevents SSRF):
$safe_response = wp_safe_remote_get( $user_url, [ 'timeout' => 10 ] );
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: raw curl, no timeout, no WP_Error integration
$ch = curl_init( 'https://api.example.com/data' );
curl_setopt( $ch, CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER, true );
$response = curl_exec( $ch );
curl_close( $ch );
$data = json_decode( $response, true );
// $response could be false on failure, no check
entries.test_step: Write code using curl_init / curl_exec targeting a slow endpoint (30-second delay). Verify it blocks the page load with no timeout. Replace with wp_remote_get($url, ['timeout' => 10]). Repeat. Page load completes in 10 seconds; WP_Error is caught.

entries.title: WordPress HTTP API: always check is_wp_error() before accessing wp_remote_* response body
entries.summary: wp_remote_get(), wp_remote_post(), and similar functions return either an array (success) or a WP_Error (DNS failure, timeout, SSL error, connection refused). AI code frequently omits the is_wp_error() check, directly accessing \$response['body']. This causes 'Cannot access offset on WP_Error' fatal errors whenever the remote server is unreachable. Always check is_wp_error() before accessing the response.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: guard with is_wp_error() before any access
$response = wp_remote_get(
    'https://api.example.com/data',
    [ 'timeout' => 10 ]
);

if ( is_wp_error( $response ) ) {
    $error_code = $response->get_error_code();
    $error_msg  = $response->get_error_message();
    error_log( "Failed to fetch API: {$error_code}, {$error_msg}" );
    return null;
}

$status = wp_remote_retrieve_response_code( $response );
if ( 200 !== $status ) {
    error_log( "API returned HTTP {$status}" );
    return null;
}

$body = wp_remote_retrieve_body( $response );
$data = json_decode( $body, true );

return $data['key'] ?? null;
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: assumes $response is always an array
$response = wp_remote_get( 'https://api.example.com/data' );
$body = $response['body'];  // Fatal: Cannot access offset on WP_Error
$data = json_decode( $body, true );
echo $data['status'];  // Never reached if network fails
entries.test_step: Write code: \$response = wp_remote_get(\$url); \$body = \$response['body']; Kill the remote server or block DNS. Call the code. Verify fatal PHP error 'Cannot access offset on WP_Error'. Add is_wp_error() guard. Repeat. No fatal; error is logged gracefully.

entries.title: WordPress options: set autoload=false for large or rarely-accessed options to prevent alloptions bloat
entries.summary: Since WordPress 6.6 an option added without an explicit autoload value is stored as 'auto', and WordPress decides for itself: it skips autoloading once the value passes a size threshold, 150,000 bytes by default and filterable through wp_max_autoloaded_option_size. Below that threshold it still autoloads, and before 6.6 the default was 'yes' regardless of size. Autoloaded options are all fetched together and cached on every page load via wp_load_alloptions(), whether or not the page uses them, so a 40KB option added without a value is loaded on every request and never reaches the threshold that would exempt it. Pass the fourth parameter explicitly: an explicit false is stored as 'off' and is honoured deterministically, where the automatic skip is a heuristic with a cutoff. The trade is one extra query when the option is actually read.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: large option with autoload=false
add_option(
    'my_plugin_large_config',
    [
        'data'  => json_encode( expensive_dataset() ),
        'posts' => get_posts( [ 'numberposts' => 500 ] ),
    ],
    '',
    false  // autoload=false: only fetched when get_option() is called explicitly
);

// Fetch on demand (single query, only when needed)
$config = get_option( 'my_plugin_large_config' );

// Small option, autoload=true is fine
add_option(
    'my_plugin_version',
    '1.0.0',
    '',
    true  // tiny string, accessed on every page, OK to autoload
);
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: large option, autoloaded by default on every page
add_option( 'my_plugin_large_config', [
    'data'  => json_encode( expensive_dataset() ),
    'posts' => get_posts( [ 'numberposts' => 500 ] ),
] );
// Every page load: +5MB memory, +extra DB query for alloptions
entries.test_step: Add an option well under the 150,000-byte threshold and with no autoload argument: add_option('big_data', json_encode(array_fill(0, 1000, 'x'))). Check the stored autoload column. On WordPress 6.6+ it reads 'auto', and the row is still loaded. Use Query Monitor to see it in wp_load_alloptions() on a page that never touches it. Re-add with autoload=false, confirm the column reads 'off', and verify the row no longer appears in alloptions on unrelated pages.

entries.title: WordPress transients: get_transient() returns false on expiry: always check and regenerate
entries.summary: get_transient() returns false when the transient has expired, was deleted, or was never set. AI code frequently assigns the result directly and accesses properties or array keys on it. Causing 'Cannot access offset on bool' fatal errors when the cache misses. The pattern requires an explicit false check and a regeneration fallback. Without it, the code is also vulnerable to cache stampede: many simultaneous requests all regenerate the expensive value at once when the transient expires.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: strict false check with regeneration fallback
function get_api_data() {
    $data = get_transient( 'my_api_data' );

    if ( false === $data ) {
        $response = wp_remote_get( 'https://api.example.com/data', [ 'timeout' => 10 ] );

        if ( is_wp_error( $response ) ) {
            return null;  // Graceful fallback on network error
        }

        $data = json_decode( wp_remote_retrieve_body( $response ), true );
        set_transient( 'my_api_data', $data, HOUR_IN_SECONDS );
    }

    return $data['key'] ?? null;
}

// CORRECT: strict false check preserves 0 and '' as valid cached values
$count = get_transient( 'my_post_count' );
if ( false === $count ) {
    $count = count_all_posts();  // 0 is a valid count
    set_transient( 'my_post_count', $count, DAY_IN_SECONDS );
}
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: assumes transient always exists
function get_api_data() {
    $data = get_transient( 'my_api_data' );
    // $data is false if expired or never set
    return $data['key'];  // Fatal: Cannot access offset 'key' on false
}

// ALSO WRONG: loose check misses valid falsy cached values
$data = get_transient( 'my_count' );
if ( ! $data ) {  // Re-generates when cached value is 0 or ''
    $data = count_all_posts();
    set_transient( 'my_count', $data, DAY_IN_SECONDS );
}
entries.test_step: Write code: \$data = get_transient('test'); echo \$data['key']; Set and then delete the transient. Call the code. Verify fatal PHP error 'Cannot access offset on bool false'. Add if ( false === \$data ) { regenerate... }. Repeat. No error; fallback triggers and data is regenerated.

entries.title: WordPress cron: wp_schedule_event() only fires on page load: use system cron for time-critical jobs
entries.summary: wp_schedule_event() registers a task in the database but does NOT run it independently. The task fires only when a visitor loads the site AND the scheduled time has passed. On low-traffic sites (staging environments, B2B tools, overnight jobs) no page load means no task execution. Using wp-cron for payment processing, webhook delivery, or time-sensitive notifications causes silent delays or complete misses. For reliable scheduling, disable wp-cron (DISABLE_WP_CRON=true) and use a real system cron job to trigger wp-cron.php.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT for non-critical tasks, wp-cron alone is fine
add_action( 'init', function() {
    if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'my_nightly_summary' ) ) {
        wp_schedule_event( time(), 'daily', 'my_nightly_summary' );
    }
} );

add_action( 'my_nightly_summary', function() {
    $summary = generate_daily_summary();
    wp_mail( get_option( 'admin_email' ), 'Daily Summary', $summary );
} );

// CORRECT for critical tasks: disable wp-cron + system cron
// wp-config.php:
// define( 'DISABLE_WP_CRON', true );

// crontab (guaranteed trigger):
// * * * * * curl -s https://example.com/wp-cron.php?doing_wp_cron >/dev/null 2>&1

// The hook registration stays the same:
add_action( 'my_payment_check', function() {
    $pending = get_option( 'pending_payments', [] );
    foreach ( $pending as $payment ) {
        process_payment( $payment );  // Now runs reliably every minute
    }
} );
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: wp-cron is not a reliable scheduler for payment processing
add_action( 'init', function() {
    if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'my_payment_check' ) ) {
        wp_schedule_event( time(), 'hourly', 'my_payment_check' );
    }
} );

add_action( 'my_payment_check', function() {
    $pending = get_option( 'pending_payments', [] );
    foreach ( $pending as $payment ) {
        process_payment( $payment );  // Must run every hour, but won't if no visitors
    }
} );
entries.test_step: Schedule a task to run every hour. Wait 2 hours without loading the site. Check if the task ran (e.g., count in wp_options) (it hasn't. Load the site once) task runs immediately. This demonstrates the traffic dependency. Fix: add DISABLE_WP_CRON=true + system cron. Wait 2 hours without loading the site. Task now runs on schedule.

entries.title: WordPress cron: scheduled events survive plugin deactivation: add register_deactivation_hook with wp_unschedule_event()
entries.summary: WordPress stores scheduled events in wp_options. Deactivating a plugin does not remove its events. They persist indefinitely, showing up in Site Health as orphaned events. When wp-cron fires an orphaned event, it looks for the callback, finds nothing, and silently fails. Always pair register_activation_hook() (which schedules events) with register_deactivation_hook() that calls wp_unschedule_event() or wp_clear_scheduled_hook() to remove them.
entries.code_example:
<?php
// CORRECT: schedule on activation, clean up on deactivation
register_activation_hook( __FILE__, function() {
    if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'my_weekly_report' ) ) {
        wp_schedule_event( time(), 'weekly', 'my_weekly_report' );
    }
} );

register_deactivation_hook( __FILE__, function() {
    // wp_clear_scheduled_hook removes ALL scheduled instances of this hook
    wp_clear_scheduled_hook( 'my_weekly_report' );
} );

add_action( 'my_weekly_report', function() {
    send_admin_email( 'Weekly Report', generate_report() );
} );

// Test: deactivate plugin, then:
// wp cron event list | grep my_weekly_report
// → should return nothing
entries.bad_pattern:
<?php
// WRONG: schedules event on activation, no cleanup on deactivation
register_activation_hook( __FILE__, function() {
    if ( ! wp_next_scheduled( 'my_weekly_report' ) ) {
        wp_schedule_event( time(), 'weekly', 'my_weekly_report' );
    }
} );

add_action( 'my_weekly_report', function() {
    send_admin_email( 'Weekly Report', generate_report() );
} );
// After plugin deactivation: event stays in wp_options forever
entries.test_step: Activate plugin that schedules cron event. Run: wp cron event list. Deactivate plugin (without cleanup code). Run: wp cron event list again. Event is still listed. Add register_deactivation_hook with wp_clear_scheduled_hook. Deactivate again. Event is now gone.

entries.title: WordPress 7.1: Classic block stays in the inserter — remove wp_classic_block_supports_inserter workarounds
entries.summary: WordPress 7.1 keeps the Classic block (`core/freeform`) in the block inserter by default. A mid-cycle plan to hide it was reverted on 7 July 2026 (Make/Core). The temporary `wp_classic_block_supports_inserter` filter was removed and never shipped in a stable release. AI-generated mu-plugins or docs that re-enable the Classic block via that filter, or that recommend the Enable Classic Block companion plugin for 7.1, are stale. No migration is required; remove the workaround.
entries.test_step:
1. Grep the project for wp_classic_block_supports_inserter — any hit is stale for 7.1.
2. Confirm no Enable Classic Block plugin is required for inserter access.
3. On WP 7.1, open the block inserter and confirm Classic is listed without custom filters.

entries.title: WordPress 7.1: prepare schemas for clients with wp_prepare_json_schema_for_client — do not mutate stored ability schemas
entries.summary: WordPress 7.1 adds wp_prepare_json_schema_for_client() (ticket #64955) to convert WordPress-style schemas into portable JSON Schema draft-04 for REST clients, MCP, and AI tooling. Core applies this automatically for Abilities REST responses and AI Client declarations. Plugins that expose schemas outside PHP validation should call it on a copy. Do not replace the schema stored on an ability with the prepared version: preparation strips sanitize_callback / validate_callback / arg_options and rewrites required-property shape for clients only.
entries.test_step:
1. Confirm ability registration stores the WordPress schema, not wp_prepare_json_schema_for_client() output.
2. On any custom REST/MCP/AI exposure path, call wp_prepare_json_schema_for_client() on a copy.
3. Assert the prepared schema has no sanitize_callback / validate_callback keys while the stored ability schema still may.

entries.title: WordPress 7.1: ability custom validation uses wp_ability_validate_input / output — REST schema callbacks are not executed
entries.summary: WordPress 7.1 adds wp_ability_validate_input and wp_ability_validate_output filters (ticket #64311) so plugins can supplement JSON Schema validation on abilities. REST-style validate_callback and sanitize_callback keywords on ability schemas are not executed by the Abilities API. Custom runtime rules belong on those filters (return true or WP_Error), not on schema callbacks copied from register_rest_route().
entries.test_step:
1. Register an ability with only validate_callback in input_schema; confirm the callback never runs on execute.
2. Add wp_ability_validate_input returning WP_Error for invalid input; confirm execute fails with that error.
3. Keep register_rest_route() validate_callback usage unchanged for real REST args.

entries.title: WordPress 7.1: use supports.background.gradient (style.background.gradient) when gradients must coexist with background images
entries.summary: WordPress 7.1 adds supports.background.gradient, stored at style.background.gradient and rendered via the background-image longhand so gradients can coexist with background images. Existing supports.color.gradient / style.color.gradient behaviour is unchanged but still uses the background shorthand, which resets other background properties. Blocks that need image + gradient together must opt into the new support, not color.gradient.
entries.test_step:
1. Opt into supports.background.gradient on a custom block that also supports backgroundImage.
2. Set both a background image and a gradient in the inspector; confirm both appear in front-end CSS as comma-separated background-image values.
3. Confirm legacy color.gradient-only blocks are unchanged.

entries.title: WordPress 7.1: remove __next40pxDefaultSize from @wordpress/components form controls (ignored; Button unchanged)
entries.summary: Starting in WordPress 7.1, @wordpress/components form controls render at 40px height by default. The __next40pxDefaultSize prop is ignored; __next40pxDefaultSize={false} no longer restores 36px. Remove the prop from form controls. Button still uses the opt-in prop and is unchanged. The deprecated Navigation component is removed — use Navigator (see Pro entry wp-7-1-editor-navigation-removed).
entries.test_step:
1. Grep for __next40pxDefaultSize next to form controls; remove those props.
2. Leave Button __next40pxDefaultSize alone unless you intentionally change Button sizing.
3. In the editor on WP 7.1, confirm form controls are 40px without the prop.

entries.title: WordPress 7.1: Post Editor canvas is always iframed — use ownerDocument/defaultView, not global document/window
entries.summary: In Gutenberg 23.6 and WordPress 7.1 the Post Editor canvas always runs inside an iframe, regardless of block apiVersion (Site Editor was already iframed). Editor scripts still load in the admin parent window, so global document and window refer to the admin page, not the canvas. Block edit code that calls window.addEventListener, document.addEventListener, window.innerWidth, or document.querySelector(".editor-styles-wrapper") against those globals breaks or silently no-ops. Derive the canvas document from the block element (element.ownerDocument) and its window (ownerDocument.defaultView), preferably with useRefEffect from @wordpress/compose. Set apiVersion to 3 and test in an iframed editor; see also Pro entries for editorStyle enqueue and admin-scoped CSS.
entries.test_step:
1. Grep edit components for window.addEventListener / document.addEventListener / document.querySelector(".editor-styles-wrapper") next to useBlockProps.
2. Replace with element.ownerDocument / defaultView via useRefEffect.
3. On Gutenberg 23.6+ or WordPress 7.1, open the Post Editor, confirm iframe[name="editor-canvas"], and verify resize / outside-click / width behaviour against the canvas.
